rationale: The current release's requirements are settled and well-specified (36/42 with explicit acceptance criteria, only 3 open questions), but a large share are explicitly flagged as likely to change frequently (promotions, pricing, UI tests), and stakeholders meet weekly and are highly available. That combination of near-term clarity plus expected ongoing churn, fed by an engaged business side, is exactly what short iterations with continuous feedback are built for.

The requirement set is now stable (only 3 flagged as changing) with strong acceptance-criteria coverage (50/58) and heavy reconciliation, dual-control and audit-trail demands, which calls for a verification level paired to every specification level rather than fast iteration. The residual risk is elicitation quality, not requirement volatility: limited vendor SME time left 11 clarification questions open and drove significant rework (14 revised), which is a reason to phase the legacy-mapping unknowns deliberately, but does not argue for continuous re-negotiation of scope with end users who don't exist here.

Full stakeholder availability removes the usual objection to iterative re-baselining, making short cycles with continuous feedback the natural fit for a low-blast-radius product.

This is a large, regulation-anchored requirement set expected to stay stable once baked into mandated rules (only 4 volatile), with strong acceptance-criteria coverage (58/65) and extensive dual-review and audit-trail obligations mapped to four distinct regulations. That profile, formal, low-churn, verification-heavy, is the textbook case for pairing every specification level with an explicit validation level rather than iterating requirements live with underwriters.

That argues for agile-paced delivery cycles operating inside formal V-model gates rather than either a single-pass waterfall or unfettered iteration on requirements that are largely already fixed by the scheme's specification.

Requirements here are unusually settled (only 3 of 24 revised, 1 conflict) against long-established, well-documented legacy interfaces, and the dominant driver is passing formal certification test scripts, which is inherently a specification-to-verification pairing exercise. The requirement set is large, stable (only 3 of 55 volatile) and closely anchored to fixed statutory filing obligations, with heavy four-eyes review and by far the heaviest documentation burden in this portfolio (32 audit/reporting requirements). A risk-driven cycle that resolves the highest-risk unknown, estimator accuracy, before committing further build, then iterates for tuning, better matches this mixed stability/verification profile than either a pure agile or a pure sequential approach.

Ten open clarification questions out of a 47-item set, driven by a low-overlap overseas actuarial team, and 12 requirements revised once legacy field mappings were understood, both signal that the biggest threat is unresolved elicitation risk around legacy data extraction rather than day-to-day scope change. A risk-first cycle that deliberately tackles the legacy-mapping and actuarial-sign-off unknowns before the full reconciliation and cutover build is committed fits better than assuming the requirement set is safe to freeze immediately.

Narrow, well-understood legacy interface, stable requirements, minimal conflicts, and a project whose entire purpose is passing formal PCI-style certification test scripts -- this is a textbook case for pairing each spec level with a verification level. Large, legacy-coupled case-management integration with low volatility, a formal post-launch change process, and a very high concentration of four-eyes review and audit-trail requirements -- architecture and verification are tightly linked to compliance obligations here. Small, architecturally simple project against a single well-understood legacy general-ledger interface, near-zero requirement volatility, and a very high concentration of reconciliation/dual-sign-off requirements -- there is essentially no architectural uncertainty to de-risk iteratively, just a need to pair each calculation/spec level with rigorous verification before each recurring filing.

This is the most architecturally complex case in the set: very high integration fan-in across many source systems including thinly-documented legacy feeds, real requirement volatility as regulators change rules, and significant cross-stakeholder conflict -- exactly the combination of technical and requirements risk that spiral's risk-driven cycles are built to manage before locking down the aggregation architecture. I'd still want basic secure-pipeline hygiene applied by default given the connection to the policy system, which is why the DevSecOps hybrids rank ahead of plain agile.

This case combines high regulatory criticality (6 mapped regulations, 36 audit requirements, 21 reconciliation requirements) with genuine volatility (14 change-prone requirements, 8 stakeholder conflicts, poorly documented legacy feeds) and very high integration complexity — the classic spiral scenario of identifying and retiring the dominant risk (source-feed reliability, cross-regulator conflicts) each cycle before committing further build effort, while still requiring formal V&V discipline within each cycle for the regulator-facing outputs.
